questions.question: Which type is the best fit for a component's `children` prop when it may receive text, elements, null or arrays?
questions.explanation: ReactNode is the widest renderable type: elements, strings, numbers, null, undefined, booleans and arrays of these. JSX.Element and ReactElement accept only a single element.

questions.question: Why does `const [user, setUser] = useState<Investor | null>(null)` need an explicit type argument?
options: Because the initial value null does not describe the Investor objects the state will hold later
Because useState cannot infer types at all
Because React requires every hook call to have a type argument
Because null is not allowed as an initial value without a generic
questions.explanation: useState infers from the initial value. With null alone it would infer type null, so later setting an Investor would fail. The type argument widens the state to Investor | null.

questions.question: A custom hook ends with `return [on, toggle];` where `on` is boolean and `toggle` is a function. What does adding `as const` change?
options: Nothing; arrays are always inferred as tuples
It makes the values immutable at runtime
It converts the array into an object
The return type becomes a readonly tuple, so each destructured value keeps its own type
questions.explanation: Without as const the return type is (boolean | (() => void))[], so calling the second element is an error. as const infers readonly [boolean, () => void]. It has no runtime effect.

questions.question: You want a `Button` component to accept every prop a native button accepts plus a `variant` prop. Which props type does that most directly?
questions.explanation: ComponentProps<"button"> gives all the props a native button accepts (onClick, disabled, type and so on). Intersecting it adds your own props. HTMLButtonElement is the DOM node type, not a props type.
